questions.question_text: Quadrilateral $ABCD$ has $AB = CD = 7$ cm and $BC = DA = 4$ cm. Diagonal $AC$ is drawn. Which proof shows that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram?

options.text: $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$ by SSS. Corresponding angles give two pairs of equal alternate angles, so $AB \parallel CD$ and $BC \parallel DA$.
$AC = BD$, so $ABCD$ is a rectangle and hence a parallelogram.
options.why: This assumes equal diagonals without evidence; equal diagonals establish a rectangle only when the quadrilateral is already known to be a parallelogram.

options.text: $AB = CD$, so this one equal pair proves that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
options.why: This uses only one pair of equal opposite sides, which does not establish both pairs of parallel sides.

options.text: The opposite angles are supplementary, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
options.why: This assumes an angle condition not given and uses supplementary opposite angles as a test; rectangles have supplementary opposite angles, but that condition alone does not prove a parallelogram.

questions.solution_text: In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDA$, $AB = CD$, $BC = DA$ and $AC$ is common, so the triangles are congruent by SSS. Corresponding angles give $\angle BAC = \angle DCA$ and $\angle BCA = \angle DAC$. Equal alternate angles establish $AB \parallel CD$ and $BC \parallel DA$, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

questions.question_text: Quadrilateral $PQRS$ has $PQ = RS = 8$ cm and $PS = RQ = 5$ cm. Diagonal $QS$ is drawn. Which proof establishes that $PQRS$ is a parallelogram?

options.text: $\triangle PQS \cong \triangle RSQ$ by SSS. Their corresponding angles give $PQ \parallel RS$ and $PS \parallel RQ$ by equal alternate angles.
$\triangle PQS \cong \triangle RSQ$ by SAS because $\angle PQS = \angle RSQ$ is given.
options.why: This treats an angle equality that must be proved as a given.

options.text: $\triangle PQS \cong \triangle RQS$ by SSS, so corresponding angles prove both pairs of sides parallel.
options.why: This puts the matching vertices in the wrong order: $P$ matches $R$, $Q$ matches $S$ and $S$ matches $Q$.

options.text: $PQ = RS$, so these two sides must be parallel; the other equal pair must also be parallel.
options.why: This assumes that equal lengths alone make individual sides parallel.

questions.solution_text: In $\triangle PQS$ and $\triangle RSQ$, $PQ = RS$, $PS = RQ$ and $QS$ is common, giving SSS. Corresponding angles give $\angle PQS = \angle RSQ$ and $\angle PSQ = \angle RQS$. Equal alternate angles prove both pairs of opposite sides parallel.

options.text: $\angle AEB = \angle CED$ (vertically opposite angles)
$\angle BAE = \angle DCE$ (alternate angles)
options.why: These alternate angles are a result of the congruence, not a given used to prove it, so they cannot be the included angle.

options.text: $\angle ABE = \angle CDE$ (corresponding angles)
options.why: This pair is not known before the congruence and is not the angle between the two given equal sides.

options.text: $\angle AEB = \angle AED$ (angles on a straight line)
options.why: These are supplementary, not equal, and they are not a matching pair between the two triangles.

questions.solution_text: The equal half-diagonals $AE = CE$ and $BE = DE$ are the two sides, and the included angle is the vertically opposite pair $\angle AEB = \angle CED$, giving SAS.

questions.question_text: The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at $E$, with $AE = CE = 6$ cm and $BE = DE = 3$ cm. Which argument proves $\triangle ABE \cong \triangle CDE$?

options.text: $AE = CE$, $BE = DE$ and $\angle AEB = \angle CED$ by vertically opposite angles, so the triangles are congruent by SAS.
$AE = CE$ and $BE = DE$, so the triangles are congruent by SSS.
options.why: This claims SSS after establishing only two pairs of equal sides.

options.text: $AE = CE$, $BE = DE$ and both angles at $E$ are right angles, so the triangles are congruent by SAS.
options.why: This assumes perpendicular diagonals, which are not given.

options.text: $\angle BAE = \angle DCE$ and $\angle ABE = \angle CDE$ because opposite sides are parallel, so AAS applies.
options.why: This assumes the parallel sides that the quadrilateral test is intended to prove.

questions.solution_text: $AE = CE$ and $BE = DE$ are given. The included angles $\angle AEB$ and $\angle CED$ are vertically opposite and equal. Thus $\triangle ABE \cong \triangle CDE$ by SAS.

questions.question_text: Quadrilateral $EFGH$ has $EF = GH = 9$ cm and $FG = HE = 5$ cm. Diagonal $EG$ is drawn. Which proof establishes that $EFGH$ is a parallelogram?

options.text: $\triangle EFG \cong \triangle GHE$ by SSS. Corresponding angles give $EF \parallel GH$ and $FG \parallel HE$ by equal alternate angles.
$\triangle EFG \cong \triangle GHE$ by RHS because $EG$ is a common hypotenuse.
options.why: This assumes right angles; a common diagonal is not necessarily a hypotenuse.

options.text: $\triangle EFG \cong \triangle GHE$ by SAS because $\angle EFG = \angle GHE$ is given.
options.why: This assumes an opposite-angle equality that is not given.

options.text: $EF = FG = GH = HE$, so all four sides are parallel in pairs.
options.why: This incorrectly equates the unequal adjacent lengths $9$ cm and $5$ cm.

questions.solution_text: $EF = GH$, $FG = HE$ and $EG$ is common, so $\triangle EFG \cong \triangle GHE$ by SSS. Corresponding angles give $\angle FEG = \angle HGE$ and $\angle FGE = \angle HEG$. Equal alternate angles establish both pairs of parallel sides.

questions.question_text: The diagonals $KM$ and $LN$ of quadrilateral $KLMN$ meet at $O$, with $KO = MO = 5$ cm and $LO = NO = 4$ cm. Which proof establishes that $KLMN$ is a parallelogram?

options.text: $\triangle KLO \cong \triangle MNO$ and $\triangle KNO \cong \triangle MLO$ by SAS, using vertically opposite angles. Corresponding angles then prove both pairs of opposite sides parallel by equal alternate angles.
Both pairs of triangles are congruent by RHS because the diagonals meet at right angles.
options.why: This assumes right angles at $O$, which are not given.

options.text: Both pairs of triangles are congruent by SSS because all four half-diagonals are equal.
options.why: This incorrectly equates the half-diagonal lengths $5$ cm and $4$ cm and supplies no third pair of corresponding sides.

options.text: Both pairs of triangles are congruent by AAS because the opposite sides are parallel.
options.why: This assumes the parallel sides that must be proved.

questions.solution_text: Equal half-diagonals and vertically opposite angles give $\triangle KLO \cong \triangle MNO$ and $\triangle KNO \cong \triangle MLO$ by SAS. Corresponding angles give $\angle LKO = \angle NMO$ and $\angle NKO = \angle LMO$. Equal alternate angles establish $KL \parallel MN$ and $KN \parallel ML$.

questions.question_text: Quadrilateral $WXYZ$ has $WX = YZ = 10$ cm and $WZ = YX = 6$ cm. Diagonal $XZ$ is drawn. Which proof establishes that $WXYZ$ is a parallelogram?

options.text: $\triangle WXZ \cong \triangle YZX$ by SSS. Corresponding angles give $WX \parallel YZ$ and $WZ \parallel YX$ by equal alternate angles.
$\triangle WXZ \cong \triangle YXZ$ by SSS, so corresponding angles prove both pairs of sides parallel.
options.why: This gives the wrong matching order: $W$ matches $Y$, $X$ matches $Z$ and $Z$ matches $X$.

options.text: $WX = YZ$, so that equal pair alone proves a parallelogram.
options.why: This uses only one equal opposite pair and does not prove both pairs of sides parallel.

options.text: $XZ = WY$, so the quadrilateral is a rectangle and hence a parallelogram.
options.why: This assumes equal diagonals without evidence and applies the rectangle test before proving a parallelogram.

questions.solution_text: $WX = YZ$, $WZ = YX$ and $XZ$ is common, so $\triangle WXZ \cong \triangle YZX$ by SSS. Corresponding angles give $\angle WXZ = \angle YZX$ and $\angle WZX = \angle YXZ$. Equal alternate angles prove both pairs of opposite sides parallel.

questions.question_text: The diagonals $PR$ and $QS$ of quadrilateral $PQRS$ intersect at $M$, with $PM = RM = 8$ cm and $QM = SM = 5$ cm. Which argument proves $\triangle PSM \cong \triangle RQM$?

options.text: $PM = RM$, $SM = QM$ and $\angle PMS = \angle RMQ$ by vertically opposite angles, so SAS applies.
$PM = QM$, $SM = RM$ and $\angle PMS = \angle RMQ$, so SAS applies.
options.why: This matches halves of different diagonals, incorrectly equating $8$ cm with $5$ cm.

options.text: $PM = RM$ and $SM = QM$, so SSS applies.
options.why: This uses only two pairs of equal sides for SSS.

options.text: $PM = RM$, $SM = QM$ and $\angle PMS = \angle PMQ$, so SAS applies.
options.why: This uses adjacent supplementary angles at $M$ instead of matching vertically opposite angles.

questions.solution_text: $PM = RM$ and $SM = QM$ are given. The included angles $\angle PMS$ and $\angle RMQ$ are vertically opposite and equal. Thus $\triangle PSM \cong \triangle RQM$ by SAS.

questions.question_text: The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at $E$, with $AE = CE = 11$ cm and $BE = DE = 7$ cm. Which complete argument proves that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram without assuming parallel sides?

options.text: Use equal half-diagonals and vertically opposite angles to prove $\triangle ABE \cong \triangle CDE$ and $\triangle ADE \cong \triangle CBE$ by SAS. Corresponding angles give two pairs of equal alternate angles, proving $AB \parallel CD$ and $AD \parallel BC$.
Use alternate angles from $AB \parallel CD$ and $AD \parallel BC$ to prove the triangles congruent, then conclude that the sides are parallel.
options.why: This assumes both parallel-side conclusions at the start, making the argument circular.

options.text: Prove $\triangle ABE \cong \triangle CDE$ by SAS and hence $AB \parallel CD$. This one parallel pair proves a parallelogram.
options.why: This stops after one pair of parallel sides; both pairs must be established.

options.text: The two diagonals have equal lengths, so $ABCD$ is a rectangle and hence a parallelogram.
options.why: This incorrectly treats the two diagonals as equal despite their different half-lengths and applies the rectangle test without first proving a parallelogram.

questions.solution_text: The givens and vertically opposite angles establish both congruences by SAS. The first gives $\angle BAE = \angle DCE$, hence $AB \parallel CD$ by equal alternate angles. The second gives $\angle DAE = \angle BCE$, hence $AD \parallel BC$ by equal alternate angles. Therefore $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

options.text: They are equal alternate angles on the transversal $AC$, and equal alternate angles mean the lines are parallel.
They are equal corresponding angles, so the lines are parallel.
options.why: $\angle BAE$ and $\angle DCE$ lie on opposite sides of the transversal, making them alternate angles, not corresponding.

options.text: They are co-interior angles that add to $180^{\circ}$.
options.why: Co-interior angles are supplementary, but here the angles are equal, so the alternate-angle reason applies.

options.text: Equal angles always mean the sides are equal, so the lines are parallel.
options.why: Equal angles do not make sides equal, and equal length would not establish parallel lines anyway.

questions.solution_text: $AC$ is a transversal, and $\angle BAE = \angle DCE$ are equal alternate angles, so $AB \parallel DC$ (equal alternate angles imply parallel lines).

questions.question_text: Quadrilateral $JKLM$ has $JK = LM = 12$ cm and $KL = MJ = 5$ cm. Diagonal $JL$ is drawn. Which proof establishes that $JKLM$ is a parallelogram?

options.text: $\triangle JKL \cong \triangle LMJ$ by SSS. Corresponding angles give $JK \parallel LM$ and $KL \parallel MJ$ by equal alternate angles.
$\triangle JKL \cong \triangle LMJ$ by RHS because the side lengths are $12$ cm and $5$ cm.
options.why: This assumes right angles from two side lengths; no right angle is given.

options.text: $\triangle JKL \cong \triangle LMJ$ by SAS because opposite angles are equal.
options.why: This assumes an opposite-angle property before proving that the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

options.text: $\triangle JKL \cong \triangle MLJ$ by SSS, so corresponding angles prove both pairs of sides parallel.
options.why: This uses the wrong matching order: $J$ matches $L$, $K$ matches $M$ and $L$ matches $J$.

questions.solution_text: $JK = LM$, $KL = MJ$ and $JL$ is common, giving $\triangle JKL \cong \triangle LMJ$ by SSS. Corresponding angles give $\angle KJL = \angle MLJ$ and $\angle KLJ = \angle MJL$. Equal alternate angles establish $JK \parallel LM$ and $KL \parallel MJ$.
